content: Mistletoe is a parasitic plant that grows on the branches of trees or shrubs. All mistletoes belong to the order Santalales and have evolved their parasitic nature independently five times. These evolutionary lineages include Misodendraceae, Loranthaceae, and two groups within Santalaceae, which were previously classified as separate families (Eremolepidaceae and Viscaceae). Despite being grouped under Santalaceae by the APG II system, the Viscaceae and Eremolepidaceae lineages have distinct evolutionary origins. The term mistletoe was originally used to describe Viscum album (European mistletoe), the only species native to Great Britain and much of Europe. It was later applied to related species, such as Phoradendron serotinum (Eastern mistletoe) found in eastern North America. European mistletoe is characterized by smooth-edged oval leaves arranged in pairs along its woody stems and waxy white berries clustered in groups of 2–6. In contrast, Eastern mistletoe has shorter, broader leaves and longer berry clusters, often containing ten or more berries. The largest family of mistletoes is Loranthaceae, which includes 73 genera and over 900 species. Some species in this family have small, insect-pollinated flowers, while others produce large, showy flowers pollinated by birds. Mistletoe biodiversity is particularly high in subtropical and tropical climates. For example, Australia is home to 85 mistletoe species, with 71 in Loranthaceae and 14 in Santalaceae. These plants grow on a wide variety of trees and can sometimes kill their hosts if infestations are severe, although they more commonly reduce the host's growth. Mistletoes are hemiparasites, meaning they have evergreen leaves capable of photosynthesis but rely on their host plants for water and mineral nutrients. The genus Arceuthobium (dwarf mistletoe) has reduced photosynthetic activity, producing only a small fraction of the sugars it needs as an adult. However, as seedlings, they actively photosynthesize until they establish a connection with their host. Birds play a crucial role in mistletoe seed dispersal. Species such as the mistle thrush in Europe, the phainopepla in southwestern North America, and Dicaeum species in Asia and Australia consume mistletoe fruits (drupes). The seeds, coated in a sticky substance called viscin (composed of cellulose strands and mucopolysaccharides), are either excreted in bird droppings or wiped onto branches by the birds. The viscin hardens, firmly attaching the seeds to their future host. The etymology of the word mistletoe is uncertain but may derive from the German words Mist (dung) and Tang (branch). In Old English, mistel was also used to refer to basil. Historically, mistletoe was often considered a pest due to its ability to kill trees and reduce the value of natural habitats. However, it is now recognized as an ecological keystone species, exerting a disproportionately significant influence on its community. Many animals depend on mistletoe for food, consuming its leaves and young shoots, transferring pollen between plants, and dispersing its seeds. The dense evergreen witches' brooms formed by dwarf mistletoes (Arceuthobium) in western North America provide excellent nesting and roosting sites for species like the northern spotted owl and marbled murrelet. In Australia, birds such as diamond firetails and painted honeyeaters are known to nest in mistletoes. These interactions enhance biodiversity, as areas with higher mistletoe densities support greater animal diversity. Thus, mistletoe can positively impact ecosystems by providing high-quality food and habitat for a wide range of animals in forests and woodlands worldwide. Uses and Mythology The leaves and young twigs of mistletoe are used in herbal medicine, particularly in Europe, where it is popular for treating circulatory and respiratory system problems and cancer. Mistletoe is also being studied as a potential treatment for tumors. In Europe, mistletoe is sometimes prescribed for medicinal purposes. Mistletoe features prominently in Norse mythology, where it is associated with the death of the god Baldr, who was killed with a weapon made of mistletoe. This myth may have influenced the modern Western tradition of kissing under mistletoe during the holiday season. In earlier times, couples would remove a berry with each kiss until all the berries were gone, at which point the mistletoe was considered to lose its vitality. The appearance and sticky nature of mistletoe fruit (viscin) have been likened to human semen, strengthening its association with fertility in pagan traditions. Mistletoe bears fruit around the Winter Solstice, a time associated with the birth of the new year, and may have been used in fertility rites in ancient Britain. This fertility connection is a more likely origin of the kissing tradition than Norse mythology, although the Saxons, who worshipped the same gods as the Norse, may have introduced the custom to Britain. The tradition of kissing under mistletoe has spread throughout the English-speaking world but is largely unknown in the rest of Europe. Christian beliefs merged with existing pagan feasts and winter rituals to create many long-standing Christmas traditions. For example, ancient Europeans believed mistletoe had magical powers to bestow life and fertility, bring peace, and protect against disease. Northern Europeans associated mistletoe with the Norse goddess of love, Freyja, and developed the custom of kissing beneath its branches. Christians later incorporated this custom into their Christmas celebrations, and it eventually became a secular tradition. In Celtic mythology and Druid rituals, mistletoe was considered an antidote to poison. However, it is now known that the fruits of many mistletoe species are toxic if ingested, as they contain viscotoxins. In Romanian traditions, mistletoe (vâsc in Romanian) is regarded as a source of good fortune. The plant's medical and supposed magical properties are still used, particularly in rural areas, a custom inherited from the Dacians. Mistletoe has sometimes been nicknamed the vampire plant because it can penetrate beneath tree bark to extract water and minerals, allowing it to survive during droughts. William Shakespeare referenced mistletoe unflatteringly in Titus Andronicus (Act II, Scene I): Overcome with moss and baleful mistletoe. Today, mistletoe is commonly used as a Christmas decoration. In Europe, Viscum album is the preferred species, while in North America, Phoradendron serotinum is used. According to a Christmas custom, any two people meeting under a hanging of mistletoe are obliged to kiss. Mistletoe is the state floral emblem of Oklahoma. Although the state did not have an official flower for many years, mistletoe was considered the de facto state flower until the Oklahoma Rose was designated as such in 2004. A popular myth confuses mistletoe with the holly tree, the most sacred tree of the Druids. According to this myth, mistletoe was cut with a golden sickle and lost its power if it touched the ground. The confusion likely arises from both plants being evergreen and bearing colorful fruits, as well as their shared history in winter traditions.
